brief.headline: Cut our price gap of ₹28.69 L/yr to match what we already pay Mars Plastics and Premier Plastic for the same items, and tighten payment to 30 days in return for faster cash.

priceAsk.summary: Close the ₹28.69 L/yr gap between their prices and what we pay Mars Plastics and Premier Plastic for identical items.
priceAsk.target: Target ₹0.81/NOS for the 28 mm PP cap (vs their ₹1.08), ₹1.38/NOS for the 30 ML HDPE bottle (vs ₹1.53), and ₹0.35/NOS for the measuring cup (vs ₹0.46).
priceAsk.basis: Mars Plastics and Premier Plastic already supply us the same items at these lower prices — we're paying ₹14.05 L extra on the cap alone, ₹7.88 L on the bottle, ₹6.75 L on the cup. Market research shows the 28 mm cap asks ₹0.85–0.95/pc typically, with room down to ₹0.65–0.80 at volume — so ₹0.81 is fair and proven.

paymentTermAsk.summary: Move from 45 days to 30 days after receipt.
paymentTermAsk.cashImpact: Frees up ₹16.02 L of cash for us, and they already take 39d to pay their own suppliers (longer than the 23d similar firms take), so asking them to tighten our terms is only matching what they do to others.

brief.financialLeverage: They're small — ₹4.11 Cr in sales — and we're nearly half of that (47.43%, ₹1.95 Cr/yr). They keep only 6.0% of every ₹100 they sell, far below the 15.0% their rivals keep, so price cuts bite hard. They owe 1.13× their own cash and their cash is stuck for 101 days (similar firms: 107d), so cash is a bit tight but not terrible. Because we're such a big customer and they're lean on profit, we can push firmly on price to close the gap to our best prices, and we can trade faster payment (which costs us ₹16.02 L in working money) for a matching discount tied to their borrowing rate of about 4.54%. But don't squeeze so hard you risk their supply — they're in the grey zone (score 1.83) and burning ₹79.14 L of free cash, so keep a second source warm.

evidence.point: We pay ₹28.69 L/yr more than our cheapest suppliers for the same rigid plastic items
The 28 mm induction-wad PP cap costs us ₹1.08/NOS from them but ₹0.81/NOS from Mars Plastics — a 33.2% gap costing ₹14.05 L/yr
We're 47.43% of their total ₹4.11 Cr revenue — nearly half their business
They keep only 6.0% profit, well below the 15.0% similar firms keep
They take 39d to pay their own suppliers, longer than the 23d similar firms take
Moving payment from 45 to 30 days frees up ₹16.02 L of cash for us

alternates.name: Manjushree Technopack Ltd
alternates.why: India's largest rigid-plastic packaging converter for pharma bottles, caps and preforms — revenue ₹2569.83 Cr, health score B (65/100) — a strong, stable second source we should qualify now.

alternates.name: Mold-Tek Packaging Ltd
alternates.why: Listed rigid-plastic leader in pails, containers and pharma packaging — profitable and robust, a credible alternate for bottles and closures.

alternates.name: Hitech Corporation Ltd
alternates.why: Listed supplier of moulded and blow-moulded packaging with broad capability across bottles and caps.

risks: They're in the grey zone (distress score 1.83) and burning ₹79.14 L of free cash — push firmly on price but keep Manjushree or Mold-Tek ready as a backup so we don't risk their supply if they wobble.
They're small (₹4.11 Cr) and we're 47.43% of their sales — if we walk, it's a huge hit to them, but also means we need them stable; balance the price squeeze with supply security.
Their profit is thin (6.0% vs 15.0% peers) — big price cuts may not stick long-term, so trade payment speed for a discount instead and lock it in writing.
They owe 1.13× their own cash — not critical, but enough to make cash tight; use that to justify the 30-day payment ask in exchange for a discount pegged to their 4.54% borrowing rate.
brief.suggestedOpeningLine: We value the relationship, but we're paying ₹28.69 lakh more each year than we do to Mars and Premier for identical items — let's close that gap and talk about how faster payment from us can help your cash flow.
